summary: This RFC documents the currently assigned values from several number series used in network protocol implementations. It obsoletes RFC 923, named Joyce Reynolds as the contact, and is historic. It was replaced by RFC 960.

plainLanguage.summary: A table of agreed numbers for network things, kept up to date by one person. Newer tables later replaced it.

questions: where to find assigned protocol numbers in 1985
how were internet numbers assigned in 1985
how many networks were assigned in 1985
subtitle: A registry of numbers and addresses used in Internet protocols.

tldr.problem: Early Internet protocols needed standardized assignments for network numbers, port assignments, and other identifiers to avoid conflicts.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 943 documents all assigned numbers in one place, organized by type (network addresses, protocol numbers, ports, etc.), and names the responsible people for making new assignments.
tldr.outcome: It became outdated quickly as the Internet grew. Assignments are now managed through multiple specialized registries, and the responsibility shifted from individual people to the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA).

today: RFC 943 is Historic and was replaced by RFC 960. Modern number assignments are managed by the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) and Regional Internet Registries, not by individual maintainers.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 943 is an official registry of all assigned numbers used in Internet protocols as of April 1985. The RFC documents network numbers, protocol numbers, port numbers, and other numeric identifiers. The responsibility for assigning new numbers rested with specific people: Joyce Reynolds handled most assignments, with Jon Postel overseeing the process.

The RFC explicitly invites developers to request new assignments from Joyce Reynolds before using a number, ensuring no conflicts. The document covers protocols documented in RFCs, some undocumented items, and notes which protocols were most widely used at the time.
sections.plainLanguage: This is like a big directory of all the agreed-upon numbers the early Internet was using. If you needed a new number, you asked one person (Joyce) to give you one.

sections.title: Internet Address Classes
sections.content:
The RFC defines the three main IP address classes that were in use in 1985. Class A networks use a 7-bit network number and a 24-bit local address (allowing 128 networks). Class B networks use a 14-bit network number and a 16-bit local address (allowing 16,384 networks). Class C networks use a 21-bit network number and an 8-bit local address (allowing 2,097,152 networks).

The RFC also defines notation conventions: Class A networks use the form nnn.rrr.rrr.rrr, Class B uses nnn.nnn.rrr.rrr, and Class C uses nnn.nnn.nnn.rrr, where nnn represents the network part and rrr represents the local or reserved parts. The document also mentions special addresses: all zeros mean "this network" and all ones mean "all hosts."
sections.plainLanguage: There were three different sizes of address groups: big ones for large organizations, medium ones for universities and labs, and small ones for individual networks. The document explains how each size works.

sections.title: Network Allocation and Categories
sections.content:
The RFC assigns network numbers to four user categories marked with a single letter: R for Research, D for Defense, G for Government (non-Defense), and C for Commercial. Networks are assigned for systems connected to the ARPA-Internet or DDN-Internet, or for independent networks using the IP family protocols.

Some network numbers are marked with a "T" to indicate a temporary transition period as assignments change. The document lists hundreds of specific network assignments, including well-known networks like ARPANET (10.0.0.0 in Class A) and many academic and research networks. As of the time of publication, there were 933 research networks, 549 defense networks, 57 government networks, and 9 commercial networks assigned.
sections.plainLanguage: Different types of organizations (universities, the military, companies) got assigned their own networks. The document kept track of who had which network and made sure no two organizations used the same numbers.

sections.title: Scope and Limitations
sections.content:
RFC 943 covers network addresses, protocol numbers, and port numbers. Some items listed are undocumented protocols. The RFC notes that it is a snapshot in time and will be updated periodically, though information changes continuously.

The RFC acknowledges that independent networks (marked with an asterisk) must apply separately for permission to interconnect with the ARPA-Internet or DDN-Internet. It also notes that assigned numbers are sometimes changed, and old numbers are kept for a transition period marked with "-TEMP" suffixes to ease the migration process.
sections.plainLanguage: The document explains what it covers and what it doesn't, and mentions that things change all the time, so it won't stay accurate for long.

sections.title: Historical Status
sections.content:
RFC 943 is now Historic. It was superseded almost immediately by RFC 960 in December 1985, and was itself an update of earlier RFCs (923, 900, 870, 820, 790, 776, 770, 762, 758, 755, 750, 739, 604, 503, 433, and 349). The centralised assignment of numbers it documented is no longer how the Internet operates.

Today, number assignments are handled by the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) and distributed across multiple specialized registries. Network addresses are assigned by Regional Internet Registries (RIRs), ports are managed through IANA registries, and protocol numbers are documented in the IANA Protocol Numbers registry.
sections.plainLanguage: This document is now historical. The Internet grew too fast for one person to manage all the numbers, so today many organizations share the job.

references.text: Postel, J., "Official ARPA-Internet Protocols", RFC 790, September 1981.
